mappings.note: The Four Sights that drove Siddhartha from the palace - the origin of the Buddhist account of suffering, so LO-150.
Avidya and attachment as the root of suffering; the central diagnosis of an ancient system of thought.
What the Jataka tales are: stories of the Buddha's earlier births (LO-136, an ancient body of literature) told to teach compassion and wisdom (LO-150).
Charvaka materialism and its denial of an afterlife - the doctrine of a named ancient school, hence LO-150.
Describes a tribe by common descent, culture, language and chiefship; the vocabulary of human diversity in LO-141 rather than a religious doctrine.

How anthropologists abandoned the labels 'primitive' and 'inferior' - the item is about a prejudiced judgement and its correction, which is LO-142's nature and sources of discrimination, applied to a diverse community (LO-141). The plain definition of a tribe took LO-141 alone.
Tribal and Hindu traditions sharing a sense that nature is sacred: a common value across systems of thought (LO-150) held across diverse communities (LO-141).
'Vid' as 'to know' and hence Veda as sacred knowledge - a fact about the texts, so LO-136, as with the other etymology items.
The role of rishis and rishikas in composing the hymns; authorship of the ancient works, hence LO-136.
What Nachiketa learns from Yama - that the atman is unborn and undying: a doctrine (LO-150) set out in a named Upanishad (LO-136).
Ahimsa reaching into thought and speech, not only deed; the fuller value that LO-150 asks pupils to analyse.

The tree analogy worked out across Vedanta, Yoga, Buddhism and Jainism: a synthesis over the whole chapter (LO-140) about ancient schools of thought (LO-150). The short version of this item took LO-140 alone.
How the Vedas were memorised and handed on, and why that is remarkable - a fact about the texts (LO-136) whose recognition as heritage is India's cultural contribution (LO-149).
Ritam as cosmic order and ekam sat as the one reality behind many names: two Vedic ideas analysed together, squarely LO-150.
Brahman, atman, rebirth and karma as the Upanishads' development of Vedic thought - the chapter's fullest doctrinal item.
Analyses ahimsa across Buddhism and Jainism and its reach beyond physical injury; a value shared by two ancient systems of thought.
Two named stories, the monkey-king Jataka and Jain Rohineya (LO-136), read for what they teach about sacrifice, leadership and reform (LO-150).
Identifies concepts the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools share despite their differences - comparison across ancient systems of thought, so LO-150.
Folk and tribal reverence for nature with named examples such as the Todas, Donyipolo and Singbonga: diverse communities (LO-141) and their beliefs (LO-150).
What region-bound janas imply about early Vedic polity - a decentralised clan landscape rather than an empire; a development of the ancient period, so LO-138.
The Upanishads' dialogue form and what it says about how wisdom was sought: a feature of the texts themselves (LO-136) bearing on the character of the thought (LO-150).

How the Sangha carried and preserved the Buddha's teaching - the institutional life of an ancient tradition. Not LO-148, since the question is about the order's function rather than about contact with lands outside India.
Anekantavada and aparigraha analysed for their bearing on tolerance and consumerism today - LO-150 asks exactly for analysis of such ideas and values.
Ekam sat read as a ground for harmony in the pupil's own multi-faith neighbourhood: an ancient idea (LO-150) applied to diversity around her (LO-141).
A modern case measured against Siddhartha's story, the causes of suffering and Buddhist detachment - every sub-part is doctrinal, so LO-150 alone.
A named tribal community's sacred Sal tree and its creator god Singbonga, set against Beteille's observation: a distinct community (LO-141) and its belief system (LO-150).
Uddalaka's clay-and-pots analogy and tat tvam asi: the brahman doctrine (LO-150) as a named Upanishadic episode presents it (LO-136).
